title: Give your opinion
when: When someone asks what you think, or you want to add your view to a discussion.

phrases.ex: If you ask me, the new canteen menu is a step down from the old one.
My honest take is that Rohan's plan is good, but the timeline is far too tight.
The way I see it, we should launch in Pune first and test the market before Mumbai.
I'd lean towards the second vendor — their quote is higher, but their delivery record is far better.
I'm fairly convinced that the drop in sales is about pricing, not the new packaging.
In my view, the board should approve the expansion only after the third-quarter numbers are in.
I would argue that rural clinics need trained nurses more than they need new buildings.

avoid.why: Common in India, but elsewhere 'according to' introduces someone else's view, so it sounds odd.
avoid.better: In my opinion, …

avoid.p: Basically, actually, what I feel is, see, …
avoid.why: Fillers pile up before the point, and listeners lose patience.
avoid.better: I think the main issue is cost.

avoid.why: Suggests people who disagree are foolish, so they stop listening.
avoid.better: I think the evidence points to …

title: Agree and add something
when: When you agree with someone and want to build on their point, not just nod.

phrases.p: Absolutely — and on top of that, …
phrases.ex: Absolutely — and on top of that, the metro station is just five minutes from that flat.
That's exactly it — Meera isn't upset about the money, she's upset that nobody asked her.
I'm with you on that — the Saturday review meetings have to go.
Building on what Priya said, we could add a Hindi version of the app for smaller towns.
I couldn't agree more — this exam schedule leaves no time at all for revision.

phrases.p: I fully support this, and I'd add that …
phrases.ex: I fully support this, and I'd add that we need a clear budget for training staff in Lucknow.
To echo that point, early screening in district hospitals saves both lives and money.

avoid.why: Indian English for 'exactly the same'; people outside India may not follow it.
avoid.better: Exactly — I think the same.

avoid.why: Sounds impatient, as if you want the other person to stop talking.
avoid.better: Yes, that's right — and there's one more thing.

avoid.why: Just echoes without adding anything, which feels lazy in a discussion.
avoid.better: I agree, and the cost data backs it up too.

title: Disagree without offending
when: When you think someone is wrong but want to keep the conversation friendly and useful.

phrases.p: I'm not so sure about that.
phrases.ex: I'm not so sure about that — Goa in May is going to be brutally hot.

phrases.p: Hmm, I'm not sold on that.
phrases.ex: Hmm, I'm not sold on that — another attendance app sounds like more work, not less.

phrases.p: I see it a little differently.
phrases.ex: I see it a little differently — I think the delay came from the vendor, not our team.

phrases.p: Can I push back on that a little?
phrases.ex: Can I push back on that a little? I don't think customers in Indore will pay extra for faster delivery.
I'd question whether a four-day week would work for the night shift at the plant.
I have some reservations about outsourcing the call centre to a vendor we haven't audited.

phrases.p: With respect, I think the data suggests otherwise.
phrases.ex: With respect, I think the data suggests otherwise — footfall in the Kochi store actually rose in March.

avoid.why: Attacks the person, so they defend instead of listening.
avoid.better: I'm not sure that's right — here's why.

avoid.why: Dismisses the idea and the person together, and the discussion turns into a fight.
avoid.better: I don't think that works, because the numbers don't add up.

avoid.p: With all due respect, you don't know what you're talking about.
avoid.why: The polite opening doesn't hide the insult; it just sounds sarcastic.
avoid.better: I think we're looking at different numbers — can we compare?

title: Accept a point, then add yours
when: When the other person has a good point, but you still want to add your own.

phrases.ex: Fair enough, but we still need someone to pick up Dadi from the station.
OK, you've got me there — I did promise to book the tickets. But you said you'd pack.
That's a fair point, but the cheaper laptops will cost us more in repairs.

phrases.p: I take your point. At the same time, …
phrases.ex: I take your point. At the same time, the Jaipur clients have been asking for this for months.
Granted, the new road cuts travel time — but the trees along the lake are a real loss.
I accept that the deadline is fixed; however, the scope can still be reduced.
While I acknowledge the concerns about cost, the long-term savings are hard to ignore.

avoid.why: Sounds like you have given up and are sulking, not agreeing.
avoid.better: Fine, that part makes sense — but here's my worry.

avoid.p: You may be right, but I am also right.
avoid.why: Turns it into a contest instead of combining the two ideas.
avoid.better: You're right on cost, and I think timing matters too.

avoid.why: Indian English pattern; 'even then' or 'even so' alone is clearer to everyone.
avoid.better: Even so, …

title: Say you are not sure
when: When you don't know the answer, or aren't confident enough to give a firm view.

phrases.ex: I'm not 100% sure, but I think the last train to Thane leaves at 12:30.

phrases.p: Don't quote me on this, but …
phrases.ex: Don't quote me on this, but I heard the board results are out on Friday.

phrases.p: I'm in two minds about it.
phrases.ex: I'm in two minds about it — the Pune offer pays more, but I'd miss Kolkata.

phrases.p: I'd need to check, but I think …
phrases.ex: I'd need to check, but I think the GST rate on this went up in April.
As far as I know, the visa takes about three weeks from the Chennai consulate.
My understanding is that the policy covers parents, but let me confirm with HR.

phrases.p: I don't have a firm view on that yet.
phrases.ex: I don't have a firm view on that yet; I'd like to see the audit report first.

avoid.why: On its own it ends the conversation; add what you do know or what you'll do.
avoid.better: I don't know offhand — I'll find out by tomorrow.

avoid.why: Sounds certain when you aren't, and if you're wrong, people trust you less.
avoid.better: I think so, but I'd double-check.

avoid.why: Sounds careless, as if the question doesn't matter to you.
avoid.better: It could go either way — it depends on the budget.

title: Ask what someone means
when: When you didn't follow what someone said, or need them to be more specific.

phrases.p: Sorry, I didn't quite catch that.
phrases.ex: Sorry, I didn't quite catch that — did you say Tuesday or Thursday?
Wait, so you're saying the flight leaves from Terminal 1, not Terminal 2?
What do you mean by 'soon' — this week or this month?

phrases.p: Could you say a bit more about …?
phrases.ex: Could you say a bit more about why the Hyderabad pilot didn't work?
Just so I'm clear, the report goes to Anjali first, and then to the client?

phrases.p: Could you give me an example?
phrases.ex: Could you give me an example of what 'more ownership' would look like in my role?

phrases.p: Could you clarify what you mean by …?
phrases.ex: Could you clarify what you mean by 'restructuring' for the Bhopal branch?

avoid.why: Sounds rude or shocked; people may think you're challenging them.
avoid.better: Sorry, what was that?

avoid.why: Common in Indian offices; elsewhere it sounds vague and a little blunt.
avoid.better: I'm not sure I follow — could you explain?

avoid.why: Blames the speaker; it is kinder to own the confusion yourself.
avoid.better: I think I've missed something — what's the main point?

title: Explain what you meant
when: When someone has misunderstood you, or you need to say your point again more clearly.

phrases.ex: Sorry, that came out wrong — I wasn't saying your cooking is bad, Ma!
What I'm getting at is that we can't keep booking the same hall every year.
What I meant was that we should delay the launch, not cancel it.

phrases.p: Let me put it another way.
phrases.ex: Let me put it another way: every extra step in sign-up loses us users.
I think I wasn't clear — I'm happy with the design, just not the colours.
My point is simply that the farmers need cold storage before they need new seeds.
To clarify, the refund applies only to orders placed before 1 October.

avoid.why: Blames the listener; taking ownership keeps things calm.
avoid.better: Let me try that again more clearly.

avoid.p: Actually, basically, what I am trying to say is, see, …
avoid.why: Fillers delay the point; say the point first.
avoid.better: My point is this: we need more time.

avoid.why: Sounds impatient and makes the listener feel slow.
avoid.better: To go back to what I said earlier, …

title: Buy time to think
when: When you're asked something and need a moment, or need to come back later with an answer.

phrases.ex: Hmm, give me a sec — I'm trying to remember which hotel we stayed at in Ooty.

phrases.p: I'd rather not give you a half-baked answer.
phrases.ex: I'd rather not give you a half-baked answer, so let me speak to the site engineer first.

phrases.p: Good question — let me think about that for a second.
phrases.ex: Good question — let me think about that for a second. I'd say about three weeks.

phrases.p: Let me get back to you on that.
phrases.ex: Let me get back to you on that — I need to check stock with the Surat warehouse.
That's worth thinking through properly; can I send you my thoughts by tonight?

phrases.p: Let me just pull up the numbers.
phrases.ex: Let me just pull up the numbers before I answer — I don't want to guess.

phrases.p: I'd like to come back to you with a considered answer.
phrases.ex: I'd like to come back to you with a considered answer by Monday, if that's acceptable.

avoid.why: Long fillers sound unprepared; a short, honest pause sounds confident.
avoid.better: Let me think for a moment.

avoid.why: Indian office English; elsewhere 'revert' means 'go back to', so it can confuse.
avoid.better: I'll get back to you by Friday.

avoid.why: Sounds as if you won't follow up; give a time instead.
avoid.better: I'll check and reply by this evening.

title: Interrupt politely
when: When you need to break into a conversation or meeting without seeming rude.

phrases.ex: Hang on a sec — did anyone actually book the banquet hall?
Sorry, quick question — is this budget per month or per quarter?
Sorry to jump in, but the cab is already waiting downstairs.

phrases.p: Can I just add something here?
phrases.ex: Can I just add something here? The Nagpur numbers include last year's returns.
Before we move on, could we confirm who's handling the vendor call?

phrases.p: If I could come in on that point, …
phrases.ex: If I could come in on that point, the regulations changed in January.
May I interject briefly? The figure on slide four should read crore, not lakh.

avoid.why: Demands attention and cuts the speaker off; they will resent it.
avoid.better: Sorry — may I add one thing?

avoid.p: Stop, stop, that's not the point.
avoid.why: Shuts the speaker down, and everyone else in the room feels it too.
avoid.better: Can I pause us there for a second?

avoid.why: In India 'doubt' means a question; elsewhere it means you distrust something.
avoid.better: I have a quick question.

title: Bring the talk back on track
when: When a meeting or conversation drifts and you need to steer it back to the main point.

phrases.ex: Anyway, where were we? Oh yes — who's driving to Lonavala.

phrases.p: Let's get back to the main point.
phrases.ex: Let's get back to the main point — do we hire one person or two?

phrases.p: That's a good point, but maybe one for another day.
phrases.ex: That's a good point, but maybe one for another day; today we need to fix the budget.
Coming back to the wedding menu, Aunty, have we decided on the sweets?

phrases.p: Can we park that for now?
phrases.ex: Can we park that for now and come back to it after lunch?
In the interest of time, let's focus on the three items that need a decision today.

phrases.p: I'm conscious of the time, so …
phrases.ex: I'm conscious of the time, so let's agree the next steps for the Kolkata launch.

avoid.why: Insults everyone's contribution, so people stop speaking up.
avoid.better: Let's focus on what we need to decide today.

avoid.why: Singles out one person and embarrasses them in front of others.
avoid.better: Let's bring it back to the agenda.

avoid.p: We are deviating, kindly come to the point.
avoid.why: Stiff office English that sounds like a scolding.
avoid.better: Let's get to the decision we need.

title: Organise your point
when: When you have several things to say and want listeners to follow you easily.

phrases.ex: Two quick things — the guest list, and who's picking up the cake.
The main thing is, Papa needs rest, so let's not plan a big party.

phrases.p: There are three things I want to cover.
phrases.ex: There are three things I want to cover: cost, timeline and who does what.
Let me start with the good news: we're ahead of target in Gujarat.
Moving on to hiring, we've filled four of the six roles in Noida.

phrases.p: The second point, and the bigger one, is …
phrases.ex: The second point, and the bigger one, is that our main supplier wants to raise prices.
To begin with, I'll outline why the Kerala project ran over budget.

avoid.p: Firstly, secondly, lastly, then also one more thing…
avoid.why: Promises an end, then keeps adding; listeners lose track.
avoid.better: That's my third and final point.

avoid.p: Let me give you the full background first.
avoid.why: People want the point before the history, and may stop listening.
avoid.better: Here's the headline, then the background.

avoid.p: Where should I start… OK, so, yeah…
avoid.why: Shows you haven't planned; a quick plan makes you sound sure.
avoid.better: Let me take this in two parts.

title: Give an example
when: When your point is abstract and an example would make it click.

phrases.ex: Like when we got lost in Shimla because Rahul trusted the map over the local driver.
Say, for example, your landlord raises the rent by 20% — what would you do?
Take the Mumbai dabbawalas, for instance — they run a near-perfect system without any app.
Here's a quick example: last Diwali, half our orders came in after 9 p.m.

phrases.p: A good case in point is …
phrases.ex: A good case in point is Kerala's literacy drive, which relied heavily on volunteers.

phrases.p: To give you a sense of what I mean, …
phrases.ex: To give you a sense of what I mean, one late flight cost us two client meetings.
To illustrate, the Bhopal plant cut water use by 30% after fixing just two pipes.

avoid.why: Stacked fillers before the example make it hard to follow.
avoid.better: For example, last month we lost two big orders.

avoid.p: Etc., etc., you know what I mean.
avoid.why: Leaves the listener to supply the example you were meant to give.
avoid.better: Here's one specific case.

avoid.why: Indian English word order, and it promises examples without giving one.
avoid.better: There are plenty — here's one.

title: Sum up
when: When you want to wrap up a discussion or check that everyone has the same picture.

phrases.ex: Long story short, the train was cancelled and we reached Varanasi at midnight.
In a nutshell, the flat is great, but the owner won’t allow pets.
So, to sum up, we're moving the launch to May and hiring two more testers.
The bottom line is we can't afford a new office this year.
So where we've landed is that Kavya leads the redesign and Arjun handles the client.
In short, the scheme works, but only where the panchayat is closely involved.
To summarise the key points, revenue is up, costs are flat, and hiring is on hold.

avoid.why: Ends without a summary, and 'doubts' means distrust outside India.
avoid.better: That's the summary — any questions?

avoid.why: Trails off without saying what was decided.
avoid.better: So, the decision is to wait until May.

avoid.p: In a nutshell, to conclude, in summary, …
avoid.why: Three openers for one summary; pick one and get to it.
avoid.better: In summary, …

title: Give feedback kindly and clearly
when: When you need to tell someone what is working and what isn't, honestly but without hurting them.

phrases.p: This is solid — just a couple of tweaks.
phrases.ex: This is solid — just a couple of tweaks and it's ready for the Delhi office.
Have you thought about adding photos? Your grandmother's recipes would really come alive.
What's working really well is how you handle angry customers — calm and clear.
One thing I'd change is the opening slide; it's too crowded to read.

phrases.p: Can I share a thought on …?
phrases.ex: Can I share a thought on the report? The summary could come first.

phrases.p: Next time, it might help to …
phrases.ex: Next time, it might help to send the agenda a day before the meeting.
I'd encourage you to present the data yourself at the next review; you know it best.

avoid.p: This is not up to the mark.
avoid.why: Says it's bad but not why, so they can't fix it.
avoid.better: The analysis is good; the conclusion needs more data.

avoid.p: Who made this? It's all wrong.
avoid.why: Public blame makes people defensive and buries the useful part.
avoid.better: Can we go through this together? A few parts need fixing.

avoid.p: No offence, but this is quite bad.
avoid.why: 'No offence' warns that offence is coming; it doesn't soften anything.
avoid.better: I think this needs another round — here's what I'd look at.

title: Say no politely
when: When you need to turn down a request, invitation or extra work without damaging the relationship.

phrases.p: I'd love to, but I can't this time.
phrases.ex: I'd love to, but I can't this time — it's my cousin's mehendi on Saturday.

phrases.p: I'm going to have to pass on this one.
phrases.ex: I'm going to have to pass on this one; my plate is full until the audit.

phrases.p: I can't take that on right now.
phrases.ex: I can't take that on right now without dropping the Chennai report.

phrases.p: That won't work for me, but here's what I can do.
phrases.ex: That won't work for me, but here's what I can do: review it on Thursday morning.

phrases.p: Honestly, I'm stretched too thin this week.
phrases.ex: Honestly, I'm stretched too thin this week — can we look at it next Monday?

phrases.p: Thank you for thinking of me, but I'll have to decline.
phrases.ex: Thank you for thinking of me, but I'll have to decline the panel invitation this year.

phrases.p: Unfortunately, we're unable to accommodate this request.
phrases.ex: Unfortunately, we're unable to accommodate this request, as the hall is booked until December.

avoid.why: Said when you mean no, it sounds like yes; a clear no is kinder.
avoid.better: I can't do it this week, sorry.

avoid.why: Blunt and final; it offers no reason or alternative.
avoid.better: I can't manage that, but I could help next week.

avoid.p: Sorry, it's not in my hands, what can I do?
avoid.why: Sounds helpless and passes the blame without helping.
avoid.better: I can't approve that, but I'll ask Neha, who can.

title: Ask for something
when: When you need something from someone — help, information, a favour or a decision.

phrases.p: Could you do me a favour?
phrases.ex: Could you do me a favour and pick up my parcel from the society office?
Any chance you could cover my shift on Sunday? I'll take yours next week.
Would you mind sending me the slides before the call?
Would it be possible to move our meeting to 4 p.m.? My flight from Bengaluru is delayed.

phrases.p: When you get a chance, could you …?
phrases.ex: When you get a chance, could you check the invoice from the Ludhiana supplier?

phrases.p: I'd really appreciate your help with …
phrases.ex: I'd really appreciate your help with the tender documents; you've done this before.

phrases.p: I'd be grateful if you could …
phrases.ex: I'd be grateful if you could share the revised contract by Friday.

avoid.why: Old Indian office English, and it doesn't say what you actually need.
avoid.better: Could you please approve my leave by Friday?

avoid.p: I humbly request you to kindly …
avoid.why: Over-formal and self-lowering; it reads like a petition, not a request.
avoid.better: Please could you share the file?

avoid.why: Sounds like an order, especially in writing; 'could you' costs nothing.
avoid.better: Could you send me the file when you can?

title: Apologise properly
when: When you have made a mistake or let someone down and want to repair it properly.

phrases.ex: My bad! I sent the wrong link to the group — here's the right one.
Sorry for the mix-up — the meeting is at 3, not 2.

phrases.p: I'm really sorry — that was my fault.
phrases.ex: I'm really sorry — that was my fault. I forgot to tell the caterer about the change.

phrases.p: I'm sorry — here's how I'll fix it.
phrases.ex: I'm sorry — here's how I'll fix it: I'll reprint the badges and bring them by ten.
I owe you an apology, Farhan — I talked over you in the meeting.
I apologise for the delay in replying; the Pune site visit ran over.

phrases.p: Please accept my sincere apologies for …
phrases.ex: Please accept my sincere apologies for the cancelled delivery; your refund is on its way.

avoid.why: Apologises for their feelings, not your action, so it sounds like blame.
avoid.better: I'm sorry I said that.

avoid.p: Sorry, sorry, but it wasn't really my fault.
avoid.why: The 'but' cancels the apology.
avoid.better: I'm sorry. I should have double-checked.

avoid.p: Extremely sorry for the inconvenience caused, regret the same.
avoid.why: A stock office line; it sounds copied, not meant.
avoid.better: I'm sorry this caused you extra work.

title: Admit you were wrong
when: When you realise your view or decision was mistaken and want to say so with grace.

phrases.p: You were right, I was wrong.
phrases.ex: You were right, I was wrong — the shortcut through Karol Bagh took twice as long.
Yeah, that one's on me — I told everyone the wrong venue.
I stand corrected — the match starts at 7:30, not 8.
I got that wrong; the deadline is the 15th, not the 20th.

phrases.p: I've changed my mind on this.
phrases.ex: I've changed my mind on this — after the survey, I think the old timings were better.
Looking back, I misjudged how long the Assam shipment would take.
I was mistaken about the second-quarter figures in Monday's email; the corrected sheet is attached.

avoid.why: Said about your own mistake, it excuses you before anyone else can.
avoid.better: That was my mistake, and I'll fix it.

avoid.why: Wins a small point and loses trust; people remember the dodge.
avoid.better: OK, my mistake.

avoid.p: OK fine, I was wrong, happy now?
avoid.why: Turns an admission into a jab and reopens the fight.
avoid.better: You're right — sorry, I was wrong.

title: Recommend and persuade
when: When you want someone to choose an option or back your idea.

phrases.ex: Trust me, you'll love it — the dosa at that place in Basavanagudi is worth the queue.
What if we tried a three-month pilot in Coimbatore before going national?
I'd really recommend the morning train — it's faster and you'll miss the traffic.

phrases.p: Here's why I think it's worth it.
phrases.ex: Here's why I think it's worth it: we save two days on every order.

phrases.p: The strongest case for this is …
phrases.ex: The strongest case for this is that customers have asked for it 400 times.
If we wait, we risk missing the Diwali season entirely.
My recommendation would be to phase the rollout over two quarters to limit the risk.

avoid.p: You have to do this, there is no other option.
avoid.why: Pressure makes people resist; reasons persuade better than orders.
avoid.better: I think this is our best option, and here's why.

avoid.why: A weak reason; people want to know why it fits them.
avoid.better: Three firms like ours tried it — here's what changed.

avoid.p: Just trust me, I know best.
avoid.why: Asks for faith instead of giving reasons, and sounds arrogant.
avoid.better: Let me show you the numbers that convinced me.

title: End a meeting or conversation
when: When you need to wrap up a meeting, call or chat without it ending awkwardly.

phrases.p: I'll let you go — talk soon!
phrases.ex: I'll let you go — talk soon! Say hi to Aunty for me.
Right, I'd better get going — the last bus to Howrah leaves at ten.
Great, I think that's everything — thanks for staying late, everyone.

phrases.p: Let's leave it there for today.
phrases.ex: Let's leave it there for today and pick up the design questions on Monday.
So, next steps: Ishaan sends the quote, and I'll call the client tomorrow.

phrases.p: Anything else before we wrap up?
phrases.ex: Anything else before we wrap up? OK, see you all on Thursday.

phrases.p: Thank you all for your time.
phrases.ex: Thank you all for your time; I'll circulate the minutes shortly, along with the revised timeline.

avoid.p: OK, so… that's all… anything else… no?… OK… bye?
avoid.why: Trailing off leaves everyone unsure whether the meeting has ended.
avoid.better: That's all for today — thanks, everyone.

avoid.p: Let's meet again and discuss further.
avoid.why: Sets up another meeting with no owner or date, so nothing moves.
avoid.better: Let's meet Thursday at 4; Asha will send the invite.

avoid.why: Abrupt; it sounds as if you're annoyed or bored.
avoid.better: I have to head off now — thanks, this was helpful.
